# CSLv3 — Caveman Spec Language, Version 3

## What It Is and Why It Exists

CSLv3 is an ultra-dense specification notation system that you and the Prismatic Hydra built over the course of about 62 hours across multiple sessions. The name "Caveman" captures the core idea: strip language down to its absolute bones. Remove every article, every filler word, every hedge, every passive construction, every phrase like "it is important to note that" — all of it. What survives is the skeleton of meaning: nouns, verbs, relationships, numbers, gates, and glyphs.

The foundational axiom is **density equals sovereignty**. In a fixed-size context window, every token wasted on linguistic overhead is a token that could have been spent on actual reasoning or holding more of a system in view. English prose carries roughly 75% redundancy according to Shannon's measurements. For specification content specifically, the redundancy is even higher because technical prose uses predictable structures, repetitive cross-reference patterns, and a smaller effective vocabulary. CSLv3 targets 5-6x compression over English for specs, which means a 128K context window effectively holds 640-768K tokens worth of specification information. More system visible simultaneously means better architectural reasoning, fewer blind spots, fewer patches-instead-of-fixes.

CSLv3 is version 3 because it reconciles three earlier versions that had drifted apart. A pasted document had an 11-file CSL-native spec suite with morpheme stacking and structured reasoning blocks. An on-disk root spec had Egyptian-style determinatives, a PEG grammar, and a complete worked example of a flora engine. A second on-disk spec had formal slot grammar, type suffixes, a BNF grammar, and tokenizer cost tables. These three sources agreed on core principles but diverged on specific operators, compound types, grammar formalization, and type annotations. CSLv3 is the union — it takes the strongest feature from each source and resolves every conflict.

## The Triple Scope

CSLv3 serves three purposes simultaneously, and this triple-scope design is the reason it looks the way it does. Every design decision had to survive all three contexts.

**First scope: human-to-AI specification communication.** When you and Claude (or GPT, or Gemini, or any member of the Prismatic Hydra) are writing game design documents, architecture specs, system specifications, or research notes, CSLv3 is the shared language. A 10,000-word English system spec compresses to roughly 2,000-2,500 tokens. Handoffs between AI instances carry more context in less space. A spec written in CSLv3 by one Claude instance can be read by another without any translation step.

**Second scope: agent reasoning substrate.** When Claude thinks internally — chain-of-thought inside `<think>` tags — CSLv3 replaces English prose. English reasoning at about 45 tokens for a typical 5-step chain compresses to about 18 tokens in CSLv3, same semantic content, 2.5x denser. That means roughly 2.5x more reasoning steps fit in the same token budget. The structured think-block format (which I'll explain below) gives reasoning a consistent skeleton that prevents drift back into verbose English, which is a known failure mode — LLMs tend to expand back into full sentences without structural reinforcement.

**Third scope: CSSL2 compiler input.** The executable subset of CSLv3 is called CSSL2, and it is a programming language. The idea is that the spec IS the code — there is no translation step from specification to implementation. CSSL2 targets x86-64 with AVX2 (no AVX-512, due to your hardware constraints) and SPIR-V for Vulkan 1.3 compute and graphics shaders. This scope is still aspirational — the parser prototype hasn't been built yet, which is why it's the top priority task in the Claude Code handoff.

## The Intellectual Ancestry

CSLv3 draws on seven specific source systems, each contributing a particular mechanism. Understanding these sources helps you understand why CSLv3 looks the way it does.

**APL and J** come from Ken Iverson, who won the 1979 Turing Award for the insight that notation shapes cognition — it doesn't just record thought, it structures it. APL assigns one glyph to each primitive operation, so `+/⍳10` (sum the first 10 integers) replaces an entire loop with accumulator, increment, and return. The problem is that APL's unicode glyphs are hostile to modern BPE tokenizers — a single APL symbol can cost 3-5 tokens. J, the ASCII-only successor to APL, solves this by providing 1-2 character ASCII aliases for every operation. CSLv3 adopts J's dual-mode principle: every unicode glyph must have an ASCII alias, and you use whichever costs fewer BPE tokens.

**Ithkuil** is John Quijada's constructed language designed purely for information density. Its key contribution is the slot-based morphology: a single Ithkuil word has up to 10 morphological slots, each encoding an orthogonal grammatical category. A famous example sentence — "On the contrary, I think it may turn out that this rugged mountain range trails off at some point" — is just two Ithkuil words. CSLv3 takes three things from Ithkuil: the slot template (every statement has fixed positional slots), the silent-defaults principle (if a value is the most common case, don't write it — only encode deviations from expectation), and multi-channel encoding (using position, nesting, and delimiter type as parallel information channels). CSLv3 deliberately does NOT adopt Ithkuil's full morphological system because Quijada himself admits it's beyond human fluency — the learnability wall is too steep.

**Sanskrit compound formation**, codified by Pāṇini in the Ashtadhyayi around the 4th century BCE, provides the compound type system. Sanskrit has types of nominal compounds that can recursively compose into larger compounds, eliminating case particles while preserving semantic relations. Later Sanskrit literature routinely uses 20-member compounds — entire sentences compressed into single "words." Pāṇini's grammar itself is a compression algorithm: roughly 4,000 rules generate the entire Sanskrit language, with meta-rules that compress rule references. CSLv3 adopts five compound types from this system (described in detail below).

**Peirce's Existential Graphs**, developed between 1896 and 1914, contribute the principle that spatial relations carry logical meaning. In Peirce's system, drawing a boundary around something negates it, and placing two things next to each other conjoins them. With just three primitives — adjacency, enclosure, and a line of identity — Peirce generates all of first-order logic. CSLv3 linearizes this for text: indentation depth serves as Peirce's "cut" (scope boundary), and items at the same indent level are implicitly AND'd together. Full 2D notation is impractical for LLM token streams, which are fundamentally linear, so this is a partial adoption.

**De Bruijn indices** contribute positional reference — the idea that variable names are for humans, and replacing them with position numbers eliminates the entire naming overhead. CSLv3 allows `$0`, `$1`, `$2` within a local scope (three levels max) to reference defined items by position instead of name. Beyond three levels or for cross-section references, you use names, because readability degrades fast with deep positional indexing.

**Lojban** contributes the unambiguous grammar principle. Every Lojban sentence has exactly one parse — no ambiguity at any level. CSLv3's grammar targets LL(2), meaning it can be parsed with just two tokens of lookahead and no backtracking. If a statement could have two readings, explicit grouping with parentheses is mandatory.

**Egyptian hieroglyphic determinatives** are silent classifier glyphs that carry zero phonetic content but disambiguate semantic category. A determinative glyph after a word tells you whether that word refers to a person, a place, an action, an abstract concept, etc. CSLv3 adopts this in two forms: domain determinative prefixes (like `§` for system/module, `∫` for continuous fields, `⊞` for spatial/discrete) and postfix type suffixes (like `'d` for data, `'f` for function, `'s` for system). They cost one or two tokens but save the 5-10 tokens that would otherwise be needed to disambiguate what something is.

## The Glyph System

CSLv3 organizes its glyphs into three tiers based on frequency and learning priority.

**Tier 0** is about 50 glyphs that you memorize first. These cover structural operators (`§` for section headers, `→` or `->` for flow/yields, `←` or `<-` for source/derives, `↔` or `<->` for bidirectional relationships), modal operators (`W!` meaning MUST as a hard requirement, `R!` meaning SHOULD as a strong recommendation, `M?` meaning MAY as optional, `N!` meaning MUST NOT as a prohibition, `I>` meaning INSIGHT or key claim, `Q?` meaning QUESTION or open issue), status and evidence markers (`✓` for confirmed/done, `◐` for partial/in-progress, `○` for pending/possible, `✗` for failed/rejected, `⊘` for unknown/no evidence, `△` for hypothetical/proposed, `▽` for deprecated/was-true-no-longer, `‼` for proven/immutable), relation operators (the five compound types plus `:` for bind/has, `::` for type-of/inherits, `=` for equals/assign), and standard set and logic operators (`∀` or `all` for universal quantification, `∃` or `any` for existential, `∈` or `in` for membership, `¬` or `~` for negation, `∧` or `&&` for logical and, `∨` or `||` for logical or).

**Tier 1** is learned as needed and covers domain determinatives (the `§ ∫ ⊞ ⟨⟩ ⌈⌉ ⟦⟧ «» ⟪⟫` set), type suffixes (`'d 'f 's 't 'e 'm 'p 'g 'r`), temporal operators, pipeline and dataflow operators (`|>` for forward pipeline, `~>` for causes/triggers), APL-derived operators (reduce, scan, each, compose), and reasoning extension glyphs used inside think-blocks.

**Tier 2** is specific to the Labyrinth of Apocalypse domain and covers physics and material glyphs like `ρ` for density, `μ` for friction, `σ` for stress, `∇` for gradient, and `Δ` for change/delta.

The critical rule is that every unicode glyph must have a declared ASCII alias. The full alias table is in the tokenizer spec. The decision of which form to use depends on BPE token cost: if the unicode glyph costs 3 or more BPE tokens, you always use the ASCII alias instead, because paying 3 tokens for a single symbol destroys the compression advantage. Most tier-0 glyphs cost 1-2 tokens and are fine to use in unicode form. Most tier-1 and tier-2 glyphs cost 2-4 tokens and should usually use their ASCII aliases.

## The Five Compound Types

This is one of CSLv3's most distinctive features and probably the thing that takes the most getting used to. Instead of using English prepositions, articles, and prepositional phrases, CSLv3 encodes the relationship between terms using the operator that joins them. There are five types, each derived from a Sanskrit compound classification.

**Tatpurusha**, written with a dot (`.`), is the determinative compound meaning "Y of X." This is by far the most common compound type, used whenever one thing belongs to, is part of, or is a property of another. `player.hp` means "health points of player." `render.pipeline.stage.vertex` means "vertex stage of the pipeline of the render system." The rightmost element is always the head — what the compound IS — and everything to the left modifies or scopes it. You read left-to-right for scope (outer to inner), but the semantic head is rightmost.

**Dvandva**, written with a plus (`+`), is the copulative compound meaning "X and Y" as co-equal items. `cpu+gpu` means "both CPU and GPU." `hp+mp+stamina` means "all three stats together." This is a flat union — all items have equal standing. There's no head.

**Karmadhāraya**, written with a hyphen (`-`), is the appositive compound meaning "Y that is X" — a descriptive or attributive relationship. `static-mesh` means "mesh that is static." `hot-path` means "path that is performance-critical." `raw-damage` means "damage that is raw, before mitigation." This is distinct from tatpurusha in a subtle but important way: tatpurusha expresses a relational connection ("of"), while karmadhāraya expresses an attributive quality ("that is"). The difference matters for parsing and for the CSSL2 compiler, even if in casual use they can seem similar.

**Bahuvrihi**, written with the tensor product symbol (`⊗`), is the exocentric compound meaning "thing having X and Y." The compound refers to something OUTSIDE itself that is characterized by the combined properties. `fire⊗resist` means "entity that has fire resistance." `red⊗crown` means "entity that has a red crown." The compound doesn't name the thing directly; it describes what the thing possesses. An earlier v2 draft used `>` for this, but that conflicts with the greater-than comparison operator, so v3 uses `⊗` instead.

**Avyayibhava**, written with `@`, is the adverbial or locative compound meaning "at/per/in the scope of X." `[redacted:social-handle]` means "per frame." `[redacted:social-handle]` means "per chunk." `[redacted:social-handle]` means "at initialization time." This scopes an operation or value to a particular context. An earlier v2 draft used `°` for this, but `@` is more intuitive, is already a single ASCII token, and is universally understood.

Compounds nest recursively without limit. `sys.render.pass.shadow.shader.frag` means "fragment shader of shadow pass of render system." When nesting creates ambiguity, explicit parentheses are mandatory.

## Morpheme Stacking

This feature is borrowed from Ithkuil's morphological slot system but scaled down to be learnable. Any term in CSLv3 can have aspect, modality, certainty, and scope suffixes appended using dot notation. The template is `BASE.aspect.modality.certainty.scope`, and you can use any subset of these slots.

The aspect suffixes are `.prog` (progressive, meaning "is currently doing"), `.perf` (perfective, meaning "has completed"), `.iter` (iterative, meaning "repeatedly"), `.hab` (habitual, meaning "regularly does"), `.inch` (inchoative, meaning "beginning to"), and `.term` (terminative, meaning "ceasing to").

The modality suffixes are `.must` (obligatory), `.may` (permitted), `.cant` (impossible), `.will` (intentional/future), and `.wont` (refuses/will not).

The certainty suffixes are `.cert` (certain), `.prob` (probable), `.poss` (possible), and `.doubt` (doubtful).

The scope suffixes are `.loc` (local), `.glob` (global), and `.ctx` (context-dependent).

So `render.prog.cert` means "is definitely rendering." `spawn.iter.may.loc` means "may repeatedly spawn, locally." `merge.inch.must` means "must begin merging." The English phrase "is currently, probably, repeatedly spawning in local scope" becomes `spawn.iter.prog.prob.loc` — five tokens instead of ten.

## The Slot Grammar

Every CSLv3 statement follows a fixed positional template with nine possible slots: EVIDENCE, MODAL, DETERMINATIVE, SUBJECT, RELATION, OBJECT, GATE, SCOPE, and META. The key principle is that defaults are silent — you only write the slots that deviate from the default value.

The default evidence is `✓` (confirmed), so you never write `✓` at the start of a statement unless you want emphasis. The default relation is `:` (is/has/definition), so a simple definition like `player.hp : f32` can drop the colon if context makes it obvious. The default gate is unconditional (always applies). The default scope is global. The default meta is none.

A minimal statement is just subject and object: `player.hp u16`. This expands to "player's health points are of type unsigned 16-bit integer, this is confirmed, it's a definition, it's unconditional, it applies globally."

A fully-slotted statement: `△ W! §render.pipeline :: forward-pass ⌈latency < 16ms⌉ [redacted:social-handle]`. This reads as "hypothetically, the render pipeline must be a forward pass, constrained to under 16ms latency, per frame."

## The Reasoning Substrate

When Claude uses CSLv3 for chain-of-thought reasoning, it follows the §P/§D/§T/§S/§C structure inside `<think>` tags.

**§ P (Problem)** states the given facts and the goal in two or three lines maximum. Just the essential setup.

**§ D (Decomposition)** breaks the goal into subproblems, written as `G → [sub₁, sub₂, sub₃]`.

**§ T (Trace)** attempts each subproblem and marks results. The notation uses `~>` for "try this approach," `✓` for success, `✗` for failure with `∵` (because) explaining why, and `→ retry(...)` for trying an alternative approach. Special reasoning glyphs include `?!` for something surprising or counterintuitive, `⤓` for diving deeper into a sub-issue, `⤒` for lifting back up to a higher abstraction, and `⟐` for pivoting to reframe the problem.

**§ S (Synthesis)** combines successful partial results into the final answer, using `⊕` for combining and `⇒` for deriving the conclusion.

**§ C (Check)** verifies the answer satisfies the original goal and checks edge cases, marking each verification with `✓` or flagging concerns with `⚠`.

Here's a concrete example. Suppose Claude is debugging a voxel engine stutter at chunk boundaries:

```
§ P
  voxel engine stutter @ chunk boundary
  hw: Intel 12-14gen + Arc A770
§ D
  stutter → [mesh.regen, alloc.spike, gpu.stall]
§ T
  mesh.regen ~> profile → 2ms ✓ not-culprit
  alloc.spike ~> heap-trace → 47MB burst ?!
    ⤓ source = chunk-LOD-promote ✓ found
  gpu.stall ~> pipeline-stats → idle 0 ✓ clean
§ S
  culprit = alloc.spike ∵ LOD-promote allocates fresh
  fix → pool.LOD-buffers + ring.allocator
§ C
  ✓ eliminates 47MB spike
  ⚠ edge: extreme LOD jumps → pool-overflow? → cap+fallback
```

The English equivalent of this would be about 45 tokens. The CSLv3 version is about 18 tokens — same information, same reasoning chain, 2.5x denser.

## The Type System

CSLv3's type system is layered from practical primitives up through dependent types.

The primitive types are the standard numeric types (`u8` through `u64`, `i8` through `i64`, `f32`, `f64`), `bool`, and `str`, plus spatial types for the game engine context (`vec2`, `vec3`, `vec4`, `mat4`, `quat`, `rgba`).

Compound types include fixed arrays `[T;N]`, dynamic arrays `[T;_]`, unions `T|U`, optionals `T?`, results `T!`, tuples `(T,U,V)`, maps `{K:V}`, references `&T`, and collections `*T`.

Algebraic types cover sum types (tagged unions defined with `enum`) and product types (structs defined with `def`). For example, `def DamageType't = enum[physical{slash,pierce,blunt}, elemental{fire,ice,lightning}]`.

The type suffix system uses postfix markers to disambiguate what role an identifier plays: `'d` for data/value, `'f` for function/process, `'s` for system/module, `'t` for type/category, `'e` for entity/instance, `'m` for material/substance, `'p` for property/attribute, `'g` for gate/boolean condition, and `'r` for rule/constraint. So `render'f` means "render, which is a function," while `render's` means "render, which is a system." You only use these when context doesn't already make the category obvious — otherwise they're silent.

The aspirational types for CSSL2 include dependent types (pi types where the return type depends on the input value, sigma types for dependent pairs), refinement types (subset types with proof obligations like "all positive floats"), and linear types (must-use-exactly-once semantics, critical for GPU buffer ownership and resource lifecycle management).

## Compression Benchmarks

The measured and projected compression ratios show that a simple constraint goes from 15-20 English tokens to 3-4 CSLv3 tokens. A struct definition goes from 50-80 English tokens to 10-15 CSLv3 tokens. An algorithm spec goes from 200-400 to 40-75. A full 10,000-word system spec goes from roughly 13,000 tokens to roughly 2,000-2,500 tokens.

The concrete example from the bridge spec: an English description of a combat damage calculation system runs 189 tokens. The CSLv3 equivalent — `raw = wpn.dmg * (atk.str/10 + 1)`, `mit = max(1, raw - def.armor)`, `final = rand(0,1) < atk.crit ? mit * (atk.crit_mult | 2) : mit`, `def.hp -= final` — runs 42 tokens. That's 4.5x compression with zero information loss.

The first thing is **CSLv3 itself**, which is a notation system. A notation is a way of writing things down. CSLv3 defines glyphs, a grammar, compound formation rules, a type system on paper, a reasoning substrate format, and so on. The thirteen `.csl` spec files in your repo capture all of that. In that sense, yes, CSLv3 as a *notation specification* is essentially complete — you can now write valid CSLv3 by following those spec files, and both humans and AI agents can read it and agree on what it means. That part is done.

The second thing is **a parser for CSLv3**. A parser is a piece of software that reads text written in a notation and turns it into a structured representation (an AST, or abstract syntax tree) that programs can work with. This is what the coding agent actually built when it wrote those Odin files — a lexer, parser, AST definitions, and test infrastructure that can consume CSLv3 text and validate it. This is real, useful CSLv3 work. It's the tooling layer that makes the notation machine-processable rather than just human-readable. Think of it like this: the CSLv3 spec is the grammar of a language, and the parser is a reading-comprehension machine for that language. Both are needed if you want computers (and by extension, compilers downstream) to actually use CSLv3 for anything beyond being a document format.

The third thing is **CSSL**, which you've now clarified is an entirely separate language project of yours that lives somewhere else and has its own goals distinct from CSLv3. ## oneAPI Level Zero — what it is

Intel's **direct-to-metal compute API** for GPUs/FPGAs/accelerators. Sits below SYCL/DPC++, above the kernel driver. Influenced by OpenCL + Vulkan but evolves independently. Open-spec, open-source reference implementation.

**Stack position:**
```
SYCL / DPC++ / OpenMP-offload     ← high-level
──────────────────────────────────
Level Zero API                    ← low-level, direct-to-metal
──────────────────────────────────
Intel Graphics Compute Runtime    ← kernel driver
──────────────────────────────────
Xe-HPG hardware (Arc A770)        ← silicon
```

**What it offers beyond Vulkan compute:**
- Virtual functions + function pointers in device code
- Unified Shared Memory (USM) with fine-grained pointer semantics
- Device partitioning (sub-device granularity)
- Power/frequency/thermal control
- Hardware diagnostics + metrics reporting
- Instrumentation + debug hooks (lower-level than Vulkan's)
- Async command-list submission model closer to DX12 bundles
- **Accepts SPIR-V kernels directly** (same IR as Vulkan)

**What Vulkan has that Level Zero doesn't:**
- Graphics pipeline (raster, vertex, fragment)
- Ray-tracing pipeline (RT-unit access is Vulkan-only on Arc currently)
- Swapchain/display/windowing
- Cross-vendor (NVIDIA + AMD ship Vulkan, not Level Zero)

## Effect on CSSLv3

**Not a replacement for Vulkan — a second parallel GPU backend for specific workloads.**

Breakdown:

1. **Graphics + RT stays Vulkan.** Radiance cascades, SVDAG rendering, point-splat compositing, ray-traced voxel lighting — all need graphics-pipeline + RT-unit access. Level Zero cannot do these on Arc.

2. **Compute-only workloads gain a faster path on Arc.** Level Zero's command-list model has lower dispatch overhead than VkQueueSubmit, exposes XMX more directly, gives bit-precise FP control (XeSS training, neural-FX, inverse-rendering grad passes, stable-fluids Poisson solvers). Measured wins on Intel hardware are typically 5-15% on dispatch-heavy compute workloads vs Vulkan compute.

3. **SPIR-V is the same IR.** Our rspirv output feeds both backends unchanged. No double codegen work — the divergence is purely at the *host submission API*.

4. **Extra capabilities Level Zero exposes:**
   - **USM explicit-migration**: `ze_external_memory_import_fd_t` for zero-copy CPU↔GPU for voxel-physics chunks. Vulkan has `VK_EXT_external_memory_host` but Level Zero's model is cleaner for unified-memory patterns.
   - **Power management**: CSSLv3 `{Power<budget_mW>}` effect (R17) gets *real* hardware backing on Intel — `zesPowerSetLimits()`. On Vulkan-only this effect is advisory.
   - **Device-to-device peer memory**: multi-GPU LoA scaling later.
   - **Sysman interface**: temperature, frequency, fan. CSSLv3 could expose thermal-throttle detection at the effect-system level.

5. **Portability cost.** Level Zero is Intel-only in practice (spec allows other vendors; none ship). Adding Level Zero as primary means losing NVIDIA/AMD paths. **Mitigation:** Level Zero as *opt-in accelerated-path effect tag*, not replacement.

## Spec changes

**10_HW.csl** — add Level Zero as secondary compute-path backend alongside Vulkan. Note iGPU/dGPU split, Intel-only scope.

**14_BACKEND.csl** (new) — host-submission backend matrix:
```
backend         graphics   compute   RT      XMX     power   scope
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Vulkan 1.4      ✓          ✓         ✓       via-coop  advisory  portable
Level Zero      ✗          ✓✓        ✗       direct    direct    Intel-only
D3D12           ✓          ✓         ✓       via-coop  advisory  Windows
Metal           ✓          ✓         ✓       coop      advisory  Apple
WebGPU          ✓          ✓         ◐       ◐         ✗         browser
```

**04_EFFECTS.csl** — `{Backend<vulkan|level_zero|d3d12|metal|webgpu>}` effect-tag. `{Power<budget_mW>}` elevated from advisory to enforceable when `{Backend<level_zero>}` + Intel HW detected.

**Where Level Zero wins for LoA specifically:**
- **Neural-FX compute passes** (XeSS2 inline, NN-upscaler, NN-denoiser) — XMX direct.
- **Inverse-fluid / inverse-rendering training loops** — bit-precise FP via Level Zero's float-controls, lower dispatch overhead when iterating thousands of gradient steps.

- **Audio-DSP unified** (R15) — Level Zero's low-dispatch-latency makes GPU-side audio-effect chains viable where Vulkan's submit-cost kills it.

- **stage2** : LoA migrated to CSSLv3
- **stage3** : C99-reproducibility anchor

You can't skip stage0 — every language that self-hosts does this. Rust did it (written in OCaml first). Zig did it. Odin did it. Even GCC bootstraps from a simpler C compiler.
